column2: Equity market value Rs 600 and debt market value Rs 400 give 60:40 weights; their historic book-value ratio is not substituted when market-value WACC is explicitly required.
column3: Market-value WACC must use the original issue proceeds rather than current market values because the financing mix was established at issue.

column2: A stated fully usable 30% interest deduction makes 10% debt cost 7% after tax; without a usable deduction, mechanically applying that shield can understate financing cost.
column3: A 10% debt always costs 7% after tax at a supplied 30% tax rate even when the question explicitly denies any usable deduction.

column2: With risk-free 4%, market return 10% and beta 1.5, CAPM required return is 13%; substituting the security's standalone standard deviation for beta changes the model.
column3: Those CAPM inputs imply 19% because beta multiplies the entire market return before adding risk-free return.

column2: Two risky assets with equal SD can produce a lower portfolio SD with correlation below one; zero correlation is not required for any diversification benefit.
column3: Diversification reduces SD only when correlation is exactly zero or negative, with no benefit at a positive correlation below one.

column2: In the standard CAPM account, well-diversified portfolios can greatly reduce firm-specific risk while retaining exposure to market-wide shocks.
column3: Increasing the number of securities removes market beta because systematic and firm-specific risks are averaged out identically.

column2: Sales Rs 1,000, variable cost Rs 600 and fixed operating cost Rs 200 give DOL=400/200=2 at that activity, subject to the linear local approximation.
column3: Those figures give DOL=1,000/200=5 because operating leverage divides sales directly by EBIT.

column2: EBIT Rs 200 and interest Rs 50, with no preference dividend, give DFL=200/150=4/3 at that EBIT under the stated model.
column3: Those figures give DFL=150/200=0.75 because financing leverage measures EBT relative to EBIT.

column2: When the stated linear models apply, DOL=2 and DFL=1.5 imply combined leverage 3, approximating a 3% EPS change for a 1% sales change around the reference point.
column3: Combined leverage is 3.5 because operating and financial leverage are additive sensitivities.

column2: Under MM's perfect-market no-tax assumptions with fixed investment policy, leverage alone does not change firm value; the result is conditional on those assumptions.
column3: The no-tax MM benchmark predicts value necessarily rises with each increase in debt because debt is cheaper than equity.

column2: The trade-off account balances debt's potential tax benefit against expected distress and related costs; observing a tax shield alone does not establish that maximum possible debt is optimal.
column3: The trade-off account prescribes 100% debt whenever interest is deductible, irrespective of distress costs.

column2: EBIT-EPS indifference identifies the EBIT at which two financing plans give equal EPS under their assumptions; it does not alone compare their total risk or firm value.
column3: The financing plan with greater EPS at forecast EBIT must have greater firm value irrespective of risk and timing.

column2: An already paid research bill is sunk in today's project decision, while using land with a forgone sale value creates an opportunity cost even if the land's historical book cost is zero.
column3: Zero book cost makes the land free for capital budgeting, while the already paid research bill is today's incremental outflow.

column2: Additional working capital is an initial project outflow and its stated terminal recovery a later inflow; recovery does not erase the time value of the initial commitment.
column3: Full terminal recovery means working capital can be omitted from NPV because its undiscounted net cash total is zero.

column2: Cash flows including general price inflation should be discounted at a consistent nominal rate; real flows require the consistent real rate under the stated Fisher relationship.
column3: Inflated nominal flows should be discounted at the lower real rate to avoid counting inflation twice.

column2: For mutually exclusive conventional projects with different scale or timing, ranking by NPV at the appropriate discount rate can differ from ranking by IRR.
column3: The project with the higher IRR necessarily has the higher NPV at every positive discount rate regardless of scale.

column2: A project with multiple cash-flow sign changes can have multiple IRRs or no economically useful unique IRR, whereas NPV remains computable at a specified rate.
column3: Multiple sign changes guarantee exactly one economically meaningful IRR because all project outflows share a common initial date.

column2: Under a single-period capital constraint with divisible independent projects, value per rupee can guide allocation; indivisibility can require comparing feasible combinations instead.
column3: The highest PI alone always identifies the optimal indivisible-project set even when its scale blocks a better feasible combination.

column2: Undiscounted payback ignores time value and flows after the cut-off, so a quicker payback need not imply a higher NPV.
column3: A shorter undiscounted payback proves a higher NPV because recovering capital earlier dominates every later cash flow.

column2: Comparing unequal-life replacement alternatives by equivalent annual cost requires compatible repeatability and service assumptions rather than automatically comparing their total NPVs.
column3: The smaller absolute present cost is always preferred for unequal-life assets even when it buys fewer years of service and repeat replacement is required.

column2: Inventory days 50 plus receivable days 30 minus payable days 40 give a 40-day cash-conversion cycle; extending payable days to 50 reduces it to 30, other things equal.
column3: Extending payable days in that example increases the cycle to 50 because accounts payable are added to inventory and receivable days.

column2: Funding permanent current assets with repeatedly renewed short-term borrowing can lower expected cost in some settings while increasing refinancing and interest-rate risk.
column3: Short-term funding of permanent current assets eliminates refinancing risk because current assets continuously turn into cash.

column2: A residual-dividend policy first finances the equity share of acceptable investment consistent with the target mix, making dividends sensitive to investment needs and retained earnings.
column3: Residual dividend policy fixes dividend independently of investment needs and finances every remaining project entirely with debt.

column2: MM dividend irrelevance relies on its market and investment-policy assumptions; it does not assert that taxes, information effects and transaction costs are absent in actual markets.
column3: MM dividend irrelevance proves dividend changes cannot convey information in any real market.

column2: Pooling receivables and issuing backed claims redistributes credit risk; tranche seniority changes loss allocation without removing defaults from the underlying pool.
column3: A senior securitisation tranche converts the entire receivable pool into risk-free assets because junior tranches absorb every conceivable loss.

column2: With Rs per dollar rising from 80 to 84, a fixed USD 10,000 unhedged payable rises from Rs 8,00,000 to Rs 8,40,000; the dollar has strengthened against the rupee.
column3: That quote change is rupee appreciation and lowers the payable's rupee cost by Rs 40,000.

column2: A dollar call can cap purchase exposure while retaining favourable spot movements at the cost of premium; a forward fixes the agreed exchange rate and creates an obligation.
column3: A bought dollar call and a dollar forward both require purchase at the contract price even when spot is more favourable.

column2: A trader buying a quoted currency pays the dealer's ask and selling it receives the bid; apparent arbitrage using inconsistent mid-prices can disappear after spreads.
column3: Using the bid to buy and the ask to sell is appropriate for the customer because those quotes identify the customer's cheaper trade prices.

column2: A dollar deposit with a bank outside the United States is a Eurodollar deposit even when geographically outside Europe; the term concerns the currency and banking location.
column3: Only a dollar deposit in the euro area is a Eurodollar because Eurocurrency is defined by European geography.

column2: A depositary receipt represents interests in underlying shares through a depositary arrangement; the issuer's equity risk is not replaced by a fixed-interest bank loan.
column3: Issuing depositary receipts converts the underlying ordinary shares into debt carrying guaranteed fixed interest.

column2: A foreign project may generate positive local cash flows while remittance restrictions delay parent receipts; the parent appraisal must reflect the timing and availability relevant to it.
column3: Positive local project cash flow is immediately available to the parent for NPV purposes even when remittance is explicitly blocked.
